subject: Mathematics
scope: Both tiers: fraction, decimal and percentage equivalence and operators. Higher GCSE/Extended IGCSE only: recurring notation and recurring-decimal conversions. Original teaching and practice, not official exam questions. Tier labels describe intended specification scope, not predicted grades. Author-proposed coverage is recorded separately from independent review and publication approval.
objectives: Convert proper, improper and mixed fractions into decimal and percentage forms.
Use a fraction or percentage as an operator on a quantity.
Convert recurring decimals to exact fractions where required.

notes.heading: Both tiers: fractions and terminating decimals
paragraphs: A proper positive fraction has numerator smaller than denominator. An improper fraction has numerator at least as large as denominator; a mixed number separates its whole and fractional parts. For instance 11/4=2 3/4=2.75. Simplify a fraction by dividing top and bottom by their highest common factor. A terminating decimal is an exact fraction with a power-of-ten denominator: 0.045=45/1000=9/200.

To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide numerator by denominator, keeping place values in the quotient. A fraction in lowest terms terminates in base ten exactly when the denominator contains no prime factors except 2 and 5. Thus 7/40 terminates because 40=2³×5, while 1/6 repeats because its denominator still contains 3. This test explains behaviour; it does not replace carrying out a requested conversion.

notes.heading: Both tiers: percentages and operators
paragraphs: Percent means per hundred. Divide a percentage by 100 to get a decimal multiplier, and multiply a decimal by 100 to express it as a percentage. Thus 0.08=8%=2/25, while 1.35=135%=27/20. A percentage can exceed 100%; it then represents more than one whole. Use the same reference whole when comparing forms.

To find 3/5 of 70, divide 70 into five equal parts then take three, or multiply 70×3/5=42. To find 12% of 250, multiply 250×0.12=30. A fraction of one quantity is not automatically the same fraction of another: specifying the whole is essential. If 18 of 24 students walk, the fraction is 18/24=3/4 and the percentage is 75%. Ratios compare parts: a red:blue ratio 3:5 means red is 3/8 of the combined total, not 3/5.

notes.heading: Higher / Extended: recurring notation and long division
paragraphs: A recurring decimal has a block of digits that repeats forever. In these notes 0.(27) means 0.272727… and 0.1(6) means 0.166666… . The usual overbar or dots on the first and last recurring digits represent the same thing. The non-repeating prefix is outside the recurring block. Finite display digits are not an exact recurring representation: 0.333333 on a calculator is not the exact value 1/3.

Long division reveals the cycle because a repeated remainder leads to the same future digits. In 5÷6, 50÷6 leaves remainder 2 after the first decimal digit 8; 20÷6 produces 3 and leaves 2 again. Therefore 5/6=0.8(3). To convert a recurring decimal back, use algebra to align identical infinite tails, subtract and solve for the original number.

notes.heading: Higher / Extended: aligning recurring tails
paragraphs: If x=0.(36), then 100x=36.(36). Subtract x to cancel the repeating tail: 99x=36, hence x=36/99=4/11. If there is a non-repeating prefix, align both the start and the period. For x=0.2(7), use 100x=27.(7) and 10x=2.(7), giving 90x=25 and x=5/18.

The subtraction must remove every recurring digit, not merely the visible first few. For x=1.2(34), 1000x=1234.(34) and 10x=12.(34), so 990x=1222. This gives 611/495, including the integer part. Substitute back by division or estimate its size. Cambridge Core does not require recurring notation or these conversions; Core learners should finish the first two sections and the Core-labelled practice.

workedExamples.prompt: Express 3 7/8 as an improper fraction, decimal and percentage.
steps: Multiply the whole part by 8 and add 7: 24+7=31.
Divide 31 by 8 to obtain 3.875; multiply by 100 to express as a percentage.

workedExamples.prompt: [Higher / Extended] Convert 0.4(18) to an exact fraction.

misconceptions.claim: A ratio 2:7 gives a fraction 2/7 of the total.
misconceptions.correction: There are nine total parts, so the first share is 2/9.

flashcards.front: How do you turn a percentage into a multiplier?
How do you convert a mixed number to an improper fraction?
flashcards.back: Multiply the whole part by the denominator and add the numerator.

flashcards.front: Which reduced denominators terminate in base ten?
flashcards.back: Those with only 2 and 5 as prime factors.

flashcards.front: How do you eliminate a recurring tail?
flashcards.back: Multiply to align identical tails, subtract, then solve.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher; IGCSE Core/Extended] Express 2 7/20 as an improper fraction, decimal and percentage.
solution: Divide by 20 and then multiply the decimal by 100 for the percentage.
markingPoints: Give the improper fraction and decimal.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher; IGCSE Core/Extended] Convert 0.35% to a decimal and a simplest fraction.
solution: Write 35/10000 and divide top and bottom by 5.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher; IGCSE Core/Extended] Calculate 7/8 of 96 and 125% of 64.
markingPoints: Use the fraction as an operator to get 84.
Handle a percentage exceeding 100 to get 80.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher; IGCSE Core/Extended] In a group, 21 of 28 learners cycle. Express this as a fraction and percentage. The cycle:non-cycle ratio is 3:1; explain why the fraction is not 3/1.
questions.answer: 3/4 and 75%; the ratio contains four total parts.
solution: A part-to-part ratio uses a different denominator from a part-to-whole fraction.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Foundation/Higher; IGCSE Core/Extended] Write 0.072 as a simplest fraction and convert 13/40 to a decimal.
[GCSE Higher; IGCSE Extended] Convert 0.(54) to a simplest fraction, showing the subtraction.
markingPoints: Align and subtract the repeating tails.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Higher; IGCSE Extended] Convert 0.3(12) to a simplest fraction. State which digits repeat.
markingPoints: Identify the non-recurring prefix and repeating block.
Form the correct difference and fraction.

questions.prompt: [GCSE Higher; IGCSE Extended] Use division to express 7/12 as a recurring decimal. Explain why writing 0.5833 is not exact.
solution: 40÷12 gives 3 remainder 4, so the 3 repeats indefinitely.
markingPoints: Show the repeated remainder and notation.
Distinguish finite approximation from exact value.

revisionGuide.summary: Equivalent forms describe the same value but may make different operations easier. A fraction of a total differs from a part-to-part ratio. Recurring conversion uses exact algebra, not rounding displayed digits.
keyIdeas: How do you turn a percentage into a multiplier? Divide by 100.
How do you convert a mixed number to an improper fraction? Multiply the whole part by the denominator and add the numerator.
Which reduced denominators terminate in base ten? Those with only 2 and 5 as prime factors.
How do you eliminate a recurring tail? Multiply to align identical tails, subtract, then solve.
